props.title: The Last Seduction
props.initialSlug: Femme fatale cons her way through deadly schemes

sections.content: The Last Seduction (1994) revolutionized the femme fatale archetype with Linda Fiorentino's ruthless Bridget Gregory, making classic noir antiheroes like Barbara Stanwyck in Double Indemnity (1944) look positively tame. Director John Dahl cranked up neo-noir's cynicism to 11, crafting a protagonist so deliciously amoral she makes Body Heat's (1981) Matty Walker seem hesitant. Fiorentino's performance deserved Oscar consideration but was deemed ineligible due to the film's initial TV airing - a criminal oversight given how she dominates every frame with calculated manipulation.

sections.content: The film sits at a crucial junction between classic noir and the sexually-charged thrillers of the 1990s. While Double Indemnity (1944) and Out of the Past (1947) had to dance around the Production Code, The Last Seduction revels in its frank sexuality and brutal psychology. It shares DNA with Fatal Attraction (1987) and Basic Instinct (1992) but strips away any moral equivocation - Bridget is pure predator, and the film celebrates her cunning without judgment.

Director John Dahl brought noir elements to small towns and highways rather than urban settings, following films like Blood Simple (1984) in transplanting noir themes to rural America. The film's success influenced later neo-noirs like Red Rock West (1993) and U Turn (1997), proving femmes fatales could thrive outside city limits. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: The film's DNA can be seen in later works like Gone Girl (2014) and Promising Young Woman (2020), which similarly feature calculating female protagonists using societal assumptions about women to their advantage. Bridget Gregory blazed the trail for these complex antiheroes, proving audiences would embrace a female protagonist who refused to apologize for her actions or undergo redemption.
